patient_note_history:
History
HPI: A 75-year-old male complains of bilateral hearing loss for all sounds that started 1 year ago and is progressively worsening. He had cerumen removal 1 month ago with moderate improvement. He reports occasional tinnitus and rare headaches. He notes that words sound jumbled in crowded places or when he is watching TV. He denies inserting any foreign body into the ear canal. No ear pain, no ear discharge, no vertigo, no loss of balance. No history of trauma to the ears; no difficulty comprehending or locating the source of sounds.
ROS: Negative.
Allergies: Penicillin, causes a rash.
Medications: HCTZ, aspirin (for 25 years).
PMH: Hypertension. UTI 1 year ago, treated with antibiotics.
PSH: None.
SH: No smoking, no EtOH, no illicit drugs. Retired veteran. Sexually active with wife only.
FH: No history of hearing loss.

exam_lines.source_text: Patient is in no acute distress.
- Pupils Equal, Round, Reactive to Light and Accommodation (PERRLA)
- Tympanic Membranes (TMs) with light reflex, no stigmata of infection, no redness to ear canal, no tenderness of auricle or periauricle, no lymphadenopathy
Weber test without lateralization; normal Rinne test (revealed air conduction > bone conduction) bilaterally.
Heart: Regular Rate and Rhythm (RRR); S1S2 Within Normal Limits (WNL); no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
- Cranial nerves: II to XII grossly intact except for decreased hearing.
- Gait: Normal; no past pointing and 8 heel to shin.

gold_additional_diagnosis:
• Meniere's disease: This condition usually presents with hearing loss, tinnitus, and episodic vertigo. It is caused by endolymphatic disruption in the inner ear. Causes include head trauma and syphilis. It can be unilateral or bilateral.
• Ototoxicity: Hearing loss caused by antibiotics will become more pronounced and may even continue to worsen for a time after the drug is discontinued. Any sensorineural hearing loss associated with these drugs is permanent. Aspirin can also cause hearing loss, but such loss is reversible with discontinuation of the drug. While workup is pending in this patient, aspirin should be withheld.
• Acoustic neuroma: It is unlikely that the patient has an intracranial lesion such as a brain tumor in the absence of any other signs. However, this diagnosis should be considered if evidence of focal neurologic deficits is found.

Paul Stout, a 75-year-old, comes to the office complaining of hearing loss.

Vital Signs:

Examinee Tasks:

1. Take a focused history.
2. Perform a focused physical exam (do not perform rectal, genitourinary, or female breast exam).
3. Explain your clinical impression and workup plan to the patient.
4. Write the patient note after leaving the room.

Examinee Response:

"Your symptoms and my examination findings indicate that you have a hearing impairment.". For now, please discontinue the use of aspirin.."
